newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mugler's fashion nightmare tops off Paris couture.
newsitem.headline: Mugler's fashion nightmare tops off Paris couture.

text.p: Thierry Mugler's nightmarish parade of dragon ladies, vampire women and wicked queens topped off a five-day Autumn-Winter haute couture season on Thursday.

To the sounds of clashing cymbals, howling wolves and Gregorian chants, models with claw-like nails and blackened lips marched out in stiletto heels and black hourglass suits reminiscent of grim 1930s Berlin.

"It's sharp and there is a customer for that kind of tailoring," said Nicole Fischelis of Saks Fifth Avenue department stores. "There's a magic to wearing his suits. They've got attitude, they're clothes with identity."

The French designer's approach to next winter for the jet-set came in a latex dress with a boa constrictor snaking down the front, the Morticia sleeves of a lady-of-the-manor coat and an aviator's jacket of tar-painted animal hide.
There were also porcupine quills on the cuffs of gloves and the collar of curvy tweed jacket, and promoter Donald Trump's daughter in a wonder-bra dress of fake monkey fur and vinyl.

A rare element of softness came in a slinky navy bouclette gown, its train lined in magenta velvet, or a maharani ensemble of mother-of pearl velveteen edged in fake mink, bucking the return to real fur seen on many catwalks this week.
The finale was typical Mugler showmanship -- a rib-crushing gown of fish scales with a bronze bustier.
"His world is one of cartoons and science fiction. When you take the clothes off the runway and put them into the showroom, they're beautiful and timeless," Fischelis said.
German designer Karl Lagerfeld's couture designs for Chanel took on the stark dream-like aura of an Ingmar Bergman film.
Pale women with long Raphaelite waves clad in smoky chiffon gowns, their empire bodices encrusted with pearls and crystals, seemed to step from a Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale.
Severe black coats hugging narrow, angular shoulders like a priest's cassock, alongside wool suits with A-line skirts over the knee, gave the collection a dowdiness that rang false.
A tree stretched its branches across a dress of organza the colour of a northern sky and chandelier crystals spilled from the narrow sleeves of a powder blue satin gown.
But suddenly, there came a grotesque coat of rasta wool, huge stoles and trains of ragged feathers, and new British model Karen Elson as a macabre bride in a black veil.
"I though it was beautiful, inventive and full of modern clothes that real women can wear," said Dawn Mello, president of Bergdorf Goodman said.

French designer Christian Lacroix showed the steamy side of his native Mediterranean in Spanish lace veils, gold arabesques on a coral brocade military jacket and persimmon satin for gowns modeled after the santons -- little clay figures -- of Naples.

A true believer in the artisanry that makes haute couture impossible to reproduced en masse, Lacroix's taste for splendour knows no limits -- a patchwork sheath with lace and sequin bodice came with quilted violet jacket, while a gown of iridescent taffeta changed from copper to turquoise in the light, its corseted damask bustier stamped with gold leaves.
Sending out two bridal gowns instead of the traditional one seemed to be the thing to do this season. Lacroix dressed one in black tulle and another in coral satin with roses in her hair.

Asked by a reporter if he wasn't overdoing it, Lacroix replied: "We need lots of wedding gowns because its the principal industry of haute couture. One often hears people say that haute couture is never seen in the street. But it is seen at weddngs. Bridal gowns are our most important orders."
American actress Demi Moore, a guest at several shows this week, described the collection as "wonderful, spectacular".
Asked whether she could see herself in any of the clothes, Moore answered hesitantly: "I think there are quite a few pieces that were very wearable."
